prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
required_recommendations: CT chest — required in all confirmed MG (here negative for thymoma)
Single-fiber EMG given diagnostic clarity already achieved by serology + RNS
Coordinate steroid plan with endocrinology — thyroid status will shift with treatment
Counsel on pregnancy planning — MG can fluctuate during gestation, ensure safe medication regimen

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

accepted: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive, without thymoma; concurrent post-Graves autoimmune thyroid disease (now hypothyroid on levothyroxine)

differential.key_features: Treated Graves disease can have residual orbitopathy; pattern here is fatigable, not restrictive; markedly positive AChR confirms MG.
Levothyroxine over-replacement could cause weakness but not fatigable ptosis with RNS decrement.
Young patient without malignancy; baseline CMAPs normal; AChR markedly positive.
Demographic possibility for childbearing-age woman; fatigable ptosis is incompatible.
Markedly elevated AChR antibodies establish organic pathology.

key_clinical_evidence: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Post-Graves autoimmune background increases MG risk (polyautoimmunity); recognize this co-occurrence rather than re-attribute MG symptoms to thyroid disease.
Childbearing-age woman: address contraception and pre-pregnancy MG management early.

patient.chief_complaint: Left eyelid drooping with double vision and jaw fatigue for 8 weeks

past_medical_history: Autoimmune thyroiditis (Graves disease treated with radioiodine 2 years ago, now hypothyroid on levothyroxine)

patient.history_present_illness: A 29-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease treated with radioiodine (now hypothyroid on levothyroxine) presented with 8 weeks of left eyelid drooping, double vision, and jaw fatigue. She first noticed her left eyelid drooping while studying late at night approximately 8 weeks ago. Initially she thought it was related to sleep deprivation from graduate school deadlines. However, the ptosis persisted during the day and worsened in the afternoon. She started experiencing double vision approximately 6 weeks ago — she described seeing two images side by side when looking to the right, and vertical separation of images when looking up. She noticed that her jaw became very fatigued when eating — by the third or fourth bite of a tough food she needed to rest her jaw for 30 seconds before continuing. Her speech became noticeably nasal after she had been speaking for more than a few minutes. She denied any difficulty swallowing liquids or solids but acknowledged food 'sometimes takes longer to chew.' She has had no headache, no limb numbness or tingling, no falls, no bowel or bladder symptoms. She initially saw a student health clinic who attributed the ptosis to allergic conjunctivitis and treated her with antihistamine eye drops without improvement. She subsequently saw an ophthalmologist who ruled out structural eyelid pathology and confirmed no proptosis — noting her prior Graves disease history, the ophthalmologist was concerned about reactivation of thyroid eye disease. However, thyroid function tests performed 2 weeks ago were normal (TSH 2.2). She was then referred to neurology. Her family history includes thyroid disease and she had a recent flare of anxiety attributed to her graduate school stress, for which she declined medication.

neurological_exam.additional: Nasal voice quality after sustained speech. Difficulty chewing — jaw fatigues after 2-3 minutes eating. NIF -61 cmH2O (normal). No respiratory distress.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Left ptosis — levator excursion 4mm. Complete fatigable ptosis left eye on sustained upgaze at 35 seconds. Right ptosis mild intermittent. Esotropia left eye at rest (left medial rectus/adductor weakness causing false impression of esotropia — actually left lateral rectus weakness). Vertical diplopia on upgaze. Pupils equal, reactive. Bilateral mild facial weakness — patient unable to close eyes tightly against resistance. No proptosis.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal. Mildly waddling after walking one block.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented. Normal cognition and language.
neurological_exam.motor: Shoulder abductors 4/5 bilaterally. Hip flexors 4+/5. Neck flexors 4-/5. Distal strength 5/5. Fatigability: neck flexion fails after 30 seconds sustained effort.
